title: Samson's Vengeance
overview: Judges Chapter 15 recounts a dramatic episode in the life of Samson, highlighting his fierce conflict with the Philistines during the time of Israel's judges. After being denied access to his wife, Samson retaliates by burning the Philistines' crops, escalating tensions that lead to violent confrontations. Despite being captured by his own people and handed over to the enemy, Samson is empowered by the Spirit of the LORD to break free and defeat a thousand Philistine soldiers with the jawbone of a donkey. The chapter closes with God providing water to revive Samson and notes his twenty-year judgeship. This chapter underscores themes of divine empowerment, human vengeance, and God's sustaining presence amid Israel's struggles under Philistine oppression.
structure:
**Verses 1-6: The Personal Conflict and Retaliation.** Samson attempts to visit his wife but is refused by her father, leading to Samson's fiery retaliation by burning Philistine crops with foxes. The Philistines respond by burning Samson's wife and her father.

**Verses 7-8: Samson's Vow and Victory.** Samson vows vengeance and defeats the Philistines with great slaughter, then retreats to the rock of Etam.

**Verses 9-13: The Philistines' Campaign and Judah's Betrayal.** The Philistines invade Judah to capture Samson. The men of Judah bind Samson and hand him over to the Philistines.

**Verses 14-17: Divine Empowerment and Samson's Triumph.** The Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson to break free from his bonds and slay a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone, naming the place Ramathlehi.

**Verses 18-20: God's Provision and Samson's Judgeship.** Samson, thirsty after the battle, calls on God who provides water miraculously. The chapter concludes by noting Samson's twenty-year judgeship over Israel during Philistine oppression.

keyVerses.text: And when he came unto Lehi, the Philistines shouted against him: and the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the cords that were upon his arms became as flax that was burnt with fire, and his bands loosed from off his hands.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the divine empowerment of Samson by the Spirit of the LORD, emphasizing that his strength and deliverance come from God, not merely human ability. It underscores the theme of God's intervention in Israel's deliverance.

keyVerses.text: And he found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith.
keyVerses.significance: Samson's use of an unconventional weapon symbolizes God's power working through unexpected means. This victory demonstrates God's provision for His servant to overcome overwhelming odds.

keyVerses.text: And he was sore athirst, and called on the LORD, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?
keyVerses.significance: Samson's prayer reveals his dependence on God even after victory, acknowledging God's role in deliverance and expressing trust in His provision amid physical need.

keyVerses.text: And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
keyVerses.significance: This verse marks the duration of Samson's judgeship, situating his leadership within the broader narrative of Israel's cyclical struggle with the Philistines and God's raising of deliverers.

characters.name: Samson
characters.description: A Nazirite judge of Israel known for his supernatural strength given by God. In this chapter, he seeks to visit his wife, retaliates fiercely against the Philistines, and is empowered by the Spirit of the LORD to defeat his enemies despite being captured.

characters.name: Philistines
characters.description: The primary antagonists in this chapter, they respond to Samson's provocations with violence, burning his wife and father-in-law and attempting to capture Samson, representing the oppressive foreign power over Israel.

characters.name: Men of Judah
characters.description: Fellow Israelites who betray Samson by binding him and handing him over to the Philistines, reflecting internal conflict and fear of Philistine domination within Israel.

characters.name: God
characters.description: Though not speaking directly, God acts powerfully by empowering Samson through His Spirit, enabling deliverance and providing water miraculously, demonstrating His sustaining presence with His chosen judge.

themes.description: Samson's strength and victories are repeatedly shown to come from the Spirit of the LORD, emphasizing that God enables His servants to accomplish His purposes even against overwhelming odds.

The chapter portrays Samson's personal vengeance against the Philistines as intertwined with God's judgment against Israel's enemies, illustrating the complex interplay of human action and divine justice.
God's miraculous provision of water to Samson after his battle highlights His care for His servants' physical and spiritual needs, reinforcing trust in God's sustaining power.
The men of Judah's betrayal of Samson reveals internal divisions and fear under foreign oppression, a recurring theme in Israel's history during the period of the judges.

historicalContext: This chapter is set during the period of the Judges, approximately the 12th to 11th century BC, a time when Israel was a loosely organized confederation of tribes without centralized monarchy. The Philistines, a sea people settled along the coastal plain of Canaan, were a dominant military and political threat to Israel. The cultural context includes tribal customs such as arranged marriages and the Nazirite vow, which Samson upheld. The political situation was marked by frequent conflicts between Israel and the Philistines, with Israel often subjugated and lacking strong leadership, leading God to raise judges like Samson to deliver His people.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God's sovereignty and grace in empowering Samson despite his flaws. Samson's victories are seen as acts of God's judgment on Israel's enemies and a demonstration of divine strength working through human weakness.

Dispensationalists often view Samson as a type of Christ in his role as deliverer, with his supernatural strength symbolizing the Spirit's power. The chapter is interpreted within the broader framework of Israel's history and God's unfolding plan for redemption.

Early church interpreters often saw Samson's battles as allegories of the spiritual warfare between good and evil, with Samson representing the believer empowered by the Holy Spirit to overcome sin and the devil.

crossReferences.connection: References the Nazirite vow and God's commandments, which Samson was under as a Nazirite, connecting to his consecration and strength.
David's use of a sling and stones to defeat Goliath parallels Samson's unconventional weapon, showing God's power working through unexpected means.
Describes God training hands for battle, echoing the divine empowerment Samson experiences in this chapter.
God's promise to strengthen and uphold His people resonates with the Spirit empowering Samson to overcome his enemies.
Samson is mentioned among the heroes of faith, highlighting his role as a God-empowered deliverer despite personal failings.

application: Trust in God's strength rather than your own when facing overwhelming challenges.
Seek God's provision in times of physical and spiritual need through prayer.
Recognize that God can use imperfect people to accomplish His purposes.
Avoid bitterness and vengeance by entrusting justice to God while acting righteously.
Be cautious of internal divisions within the community of faith and strive for unity.
Remember that God's Spirit empowers believers to overcome spiritual battles.
conclusion: Judges Chapter 15 powerfully illustrates the dynamic interplay of human frailty, divine empowerment, and God's sustaining grace in the midst of conflict. Samson's story reveals that even flawed individuals can be used by God to accomplish His purposes when empowered by His Spirit. The chapter challenges believers to trust in God's provision and strength, to seek His justice, and to remain faithful amid opposition. Its themes of deliverance, vengeance, and divine sustenance continue to inspire and instruct Christians today in their spiritual battles and reliance on God.
timeline: c. 1100 BC - Period of the Judges

Ropes or cords used for binding.

outline.heading: Samson Denied Access to His Wife and Retaliates
outline.description: Samson attempts to visit his wife but is refused by her father, leading him to catch foxes and burn the Philistines' crops. The Philistines retaliate by burning Samson's wife and her father, escalating the conflict.

outline.heading: Samson’s Vow and Defeat of the Philistines
outline.description: Samson vows to be avenged and slaughters many Philistines, then retreats to the rock of Etam for safety.

outline.heading: Philistines Invade Judah and Judah Betrays Samson
outline.description: The Philistines invade Judah to capture Samson. The men of Judah bind Samson and hand him over to the Philistines, showing internal strife and fear.

outline.heading: Samson Empowered by God and Defeats Philistines
outline.description: The Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson to break free from his bonds and kill a thousand Philistines with a donkey’s jawbone, marking a miraculous victory.

outline.heading: God Provides Water and Samson’s Judgeship
outline.description: After the battle, Samson is thirsty and prays to God, who provides water miraculously. The chapter concludes by noting Samson’s twenty-year judgeship during Philistine oppression.
